newsitem.title: USA: Green groups say EPA air plan flawed, but good step.
newsitem.headline: Green groups say EPA air plan flawed, but good step.

text.p: Environmentalists on Thursday said the Clinton administration's proposal for stricter air standards still was too weak and would allow some 40,000 premature deaths a year from lung ailments.

The Environmental Working Group (EWG) in a briefing also said the Environmental Protection Agency's suggested scheme for enforcing the new standard, which would involve averaging pollution from different locations, could allow pockets of unsafe air to persist.

While saying the administration deserved credit for pushing stricter standards againt smog and soot that spews from industry and utility smokestacks and vehicle tailpipes, several environmental groups at a news briefing said the proposal had shortcomings and should be strengthened.
"What the public and the EPA must decide is how many people should die prematurely each year from the simple act of breathing," Richard Wiles of the EWG said.
Industries in a coalition fighting stronger pollution rules meanwhile accused environmental and health advocates of using "scare tactics" and unsound science in promoting stiffer standards.
"Science has yet to establish any direct linkage between small particle exposure and increased mortality rates," the coalition of industries including oil, steel and automakers said in a statement.
"... despite scare tactics being used by proponents (of the EPA plan), the fact remains these costly proposals will not produce any significant improvement in public health," the statement said.
With public hearings on the issue set for four cities across the country next week, Congress members also voiced concerns.

Senate Small Business Committee Chairman Christopher Bond, a Missouri Republican, and ranking committee Democrat Dale Bumpers of Arkansas in a letter to EPA Administrator Carol Browner, said the agency did not comply with a new law requiring it to analyze a rule's potential economic impact on small business.
Browner said in a statement that views of small business would be considered before the agency issued a final rule in June.
